presenceLabel: Adena area (archaeological culture, not a tribe)
presenceNote: An archaeological culture, not a tribe: burial mounds and earthworks that archaeologists group as Adena. Kentucky about 500 BCE–250 CE; Ohio about 800 BCE–100 CE. Drawn: eight whole Kentucky counties named for documented sites, plus Ross County, Ohio (the Adena Mound, the type site). A general area, not a boundary; the rest of Ohio is not drawn and no site locations are shown. Medium confidence for years, medium-low for area.
overlapNote: Other Woodland groups lived at the same time (Hopewell-style traits appear at some sites); no mapped nation overlaps in time because Adena ends about AD 250. Ross County, Ohio, lies outside Kentucky.
basis: Kentucky Archaeological Survey Adena booklet and Woodland-period chapter, the Ohio History Connection, the National Register entry for the Adena Mound, and Wikipedia (the culture article and its list of Adena sites).

eras.label: c.800–501 BCE · Ohio (type-site county)
eras.text: Adena is an archaeological culture, a group of burial mounds, earthworks and related sites that archaeologists define from what they share; it is not a tribe, and no descent from or link to any later people is claimed. The Ohio History Connection dates Adena mound-building in Ohio from 800 BC to AD 100. Only Ross County, Ohio, is tinted, because it holds the Adena Mound at Chillicothe, the type site (National Register of Historic Places). Ohio is the centre of the culture, but the rest of its Ohio extent is not drawn, and no Kentucky site is dated this early in the sources used here. The tint is one whole county: a general area, not a boundary. The c.800 BCE start is the agency's round date.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · Ohio type-site county only

eras.label: 500 BCE–100 CE · Kentucky and Ohio
eras.text: Adena is an archaeological culture, a group of burial mounds, earthworks and related sites that archaeologists define from what they share; it is not a tribe, and no descent from or link to any later people is claimed. The Kentucky Archaeological Survey dates Adena in Kentucky to about 500 BC to AD 250 (the Adena booklet says to AD 200), with its core area in the Central Bluegrass and earthworks also in the Northern and Eastern Bluegrass, along the Salt River and the lower Big Sandy. The tint is eight whole Kentucky counties named for documented mounds or earthworks (Fayette, Montgomery, Bath, Boone, Madison, Mason, Bourbon, Greenup) plus Ross County, Ohio, for the type site. The sources list sites by name rather than drawing an area, so this is a general area, not a boundary, and many mounds have been excavated or destroyed; no site locations are shown.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · site counties, not a boundary

eras.label: 101–250 CE · Kentucky
eras.text: Adena is an archaeological culture, a group of burial mounds, earthworks and related sites that archaeologists define from what they share; it is not a tribe, and no descent from or link to any later people is claimed. After about AD 100 the Ohio sources used here no longer date Adena, so only Kentucky is tinted. The Kentucky Archaeological Survey places the end of Adena in Kentucky around AD 250. The tint is the same eight whole Kentucky counties named for documented mounds or earthworks: a general area, not a boundary.
